Overview](#1-overview)\n    10→  - [2. New model bringup flow in TTNN](#2-new-model-bringup-flow-in-ttnn)\n    11→    - [2.1 Recommended steps for model bringup](#21-recommented-steps-for-model-bringup)\n    12→    - [2.2 Create a model Card](#22-create-a-model-card)\n    13→    - [2.3 Using the reference model in Torch](#23-using-the-reference-model-in-torch)\n    14→    - [2.4 Create the torch model graph](#24-create-the-torch-model-graph)\n    15→    - [2.5 Extract the model summary](#25-extract-the-model-summary)\n    16→    - [2.6 Create issues for potential bugs or missing TTNN ops](#26-create-issues-for-potential-bugs-or-missing-ttnn-ops)\n    17→  - [3. End to end model performance](#4-end-to-end-model-performance)\n    22→    - [4.1 Performance sheet](#41-performance-sheet)\n    23→    - [4.2 Visualizer](#42-visualizer--)\n    24→    - [4.3 Trace and 2cq](#44-trace-and-2cq)\n    25→  - [5. Conclusion](#5-conclusion)\n    26→\n    27→\n    28→\n    29→## 1. Overview\n    30→\n    31→[TTNN](https://docs.tenstorrent.com/tt-metal/latest/ttnn/index.html) is a library that provides a user-friendly interface to operations that run on TensTorrent’s hardware using tt-metal programming model. ttnn is designed to be intuitive to an user that is familiar with [PyTorch](https://pytorch.org/). This report will walk you through our recommented steps to bringup deep learning models that can run efficently on Tenstorrent's hardware using the TTNN library. We will suggest a flow with code examples and diagrams to enable new users interested in bringing up their own models.\n    32→\n    33→## 2. New model bringup flow in TTNN\n    34→\n    35→### 2.1 Recommended steps for model bringup\n    36→  - The following diagram illustrates our recommened steps for a new model bring-up on TTNN.\n    37→![New model bring-up flow](images/Flow.png)\n    38→  - In the following sections we will dive deeper into each step with examples.\n    39→\n    40→### 2.2 Create a model Card\n    41→  - The model card may be created as a github issue or a google sheet/google doc. It is meant to proivde the high-level details of the model.\n    42→![create a model card](images/model_card.png)\n    43→\n    44→### 2.3 Using the reference model in Torch\n    45→  - If the model is publicly available, you may include a link to the reference model. Here is an example: [yolov4_reference_model](https://github.com/Tianxiaomo/pytorch-YOLOv4/blob/master/models.py)\n    46→\n    47→### 2.4 Create the torch model graph\n    48→  - The next step is to generate the pytorch model graph. If you already have access to a torch reference model, you may generate it using the existing code. Otherwise, you will need to implement a torch model first as this will be used later on for comparision to the TTNN model ouputs any ways. Here is an example: [yolov4_torch_graph](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/17112021/model_pytorch_yolov4.gv.pdf)\n    49→\n    50→### 2.5 Extract the model summary\n    51→  - Generate a torch model summary in order to extract the arguments and parameters of each op in the torch implementation. Here is a reference code for generating the model summary: [yolov4_model_summary_generation_script](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/models/demos/yolov4/reference/yolov4_summary.py)\n    52→  - Using the reference graph and model summary, document the modules and all torch ops required for the model implementation. For instance, in yolo-v4, there are 9 modules; Resblock, Downsample1 (DS1), DS2, DS3, DS4, DS5, Neck, Head and Yolov4. And, the following ops: Conv2d, Maxpool, concat, batch_norm, Mish, leakyRelu, upsample, add. The model summary will include the parameters of each op.\n    53→\n    54→### 2.6 Create issues for potential bugs or missing TTNN ops\n    55→  - As you extract all torch ops using the torch graph and model summary in the previous step, you will need to create the equivalant TTNN unit tests per op in the next step. You may realize that some of the ops might not have a TTNN implementation yet. In such cases, you may file a github issue to reqest an implementation. Here is an example where convTranspose2D was not available. An issue was created and the op got implemented by Metalium team. [missing TTNN convTranspose2D github issue](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/issues/6326)\n    56→\n    57→\n    58→## 3. End to end model in TTNN\n    59→  - Once, you have created a model card and extracted all required details from a torch implmentation of the model, you can use the following diagram that breaks down the steps to have a full model implmentation in TTNN:\n    60→![Model bring-up](images/model_bringup.png)\n    61→  - In the following sections we will dive deep into each step.\n    62→\n    63→## 3.1 Create TTNN unit tests per module and per op\n    64→  - It is highly recommended to start by creating TTNN unit tests per op in your model. Then move on to create pytests per module in your model. Here you can find examples of writing unit tests for the maxpool op: [unit tests for maxpool](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tests/ttnn/unit_tests/operations/pool/test_maxpool2d.py)\n    65→  - The unit tests per op will use [PCC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearson_correlation_coefficient) to ensure the TTNN op's output is an accurate match with that of torch.\n    66→  - It will also enable the user to try different settings and TTNN knobs available for the op and analyze the performance of the op and optimize it when possible. The optimization and range of knobs available to the user per op is a more advanced topic. However, once you develop a good command of the over all bring up process, you may refer to the [yolov4_tech_report](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tech_reports/YoloV4-TTNN/yolov4.md) to learn more. The existing unit tests such as the conv2d unit tests [here](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tests/ttnn/unit_tests/operations/conv/test_conv2d.py) are also a great starting point. You may explore more unit tests for different ops under [operations unit tests](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/tree/main/tests/ttnn/unit_tests/operations).\n    67→  - Once you have unit tests for all the ops in a module of your model, for instance, all the ops in Downsample1 module of yolov4, you may proceed with the module bring up in TTNN. At this stage, all ops might be supported on TTNN and the unit tests may pass for all which would be great. However, it might happen that an op does not have a kernel implementation for TTNN yet or it might fail with the confifurations you need. In such cases, you may proceed with creating detailed git hub issues to request support for those and fall back to torch for those ops unit the support is added in TTNN.\n    68→  - Here is an example of the downsample1 module implementation of YOLO-v4 in torch: [DS1 in torch](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/models/demos/yolov4/reference/downsample1.py). And the TTNN implmentation of the same module is here: [DS1 in TTNN](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/models/demos/yolov4/tt/downsample1.py)\n    69→The diagram below illustrates the corresponding Downsample1 module:\n    70→![Downsample1 Diagram](images/Downsample1_diagram.png)\n    71→\n    72→## 3.2 PCC\n    73→  - Similar to individual ops unit tests, user is highly encouraged to check per module [PCC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearson_correlation_coefficient) to ensure the accueacy of per module output from the TTNN implmenetation. Here is an example of it in yolov4 implementation: [PCC assertion](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/models/demos/yolov4/tests/pcc/test_ttnn_yolov4.py#L69).\n    74→\n    75→\n    76→## 3.3 Optimization\n    77→  - When writing TTNN models, there can be several levels of optimization. We can break them down into 3 stages. At the first stage, optimization can be acheived at per-op level. For instance, for a convolution op:\n    78→  - STAGE 1:\n    79→  - Based on the height, width and number of chanels, you may decide the sharding stratefy (height-sharding, width-sharding, or block-sharding). You may refer to the documentation on convolutions for more details here: [Conv sharding strategy](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tech_reports/CNNs/ttcnn.md#sharding) [sharding strategy explained in yolov4-tech report](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tech_reports/YoloV4-TTNN/yolov4.md#24-use-best-shardlayout-for-convolutio)\n    80→  - At the op-level, you may also optimize by selecting the optimal data type such as bfloat8_b over bfloat_16 when possible. Here is another example of it in yolo-v4 tech report: [data-type optimization](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tech_reports/YoloV4-TTNN/yolov4.md#23-data-type-optimization)\n    81→  - At the op-level, another argument is the math_fidelity. Always set the math_fidelity=ttnn.MathFidelity.LoFi unless you observe noticeable drop in PCC.\n    82→  - At the module-level, there are parameters to optimize based on your module graph. For instance, for the convolution op, you should set the deallocate_activation to True if you will not be using the input tensor to the conv anywhere else on the model graph. Please refer to the example here: [Yolo-v4 architecture](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tech_reports/YoloV4-TTNN/yolov4.md#3-yolov4-architecture).\n    83→  - At the module-level as well as the full-model-level, there are intial oprimizations you may consider, for instance, when the module or the full model consists of cosequtive ops, idally there should be minimal changes in sharding strategy between ops. For instance, if the model starts with width-sharding op, it would be ideal to keep the same strategy for the following op as reshards can be expensive. So it is recommended to find the best sharding strategies per op. However, once you have a module implementation, you may generate the perf sheet (this will be covered on a following section of this reort) to analyze the device run-time of the full module/full model and identify where keeping the same sharding strategy could be beneficial looking at the end to end device time versus doing reshareds between ops.\n    84→\n    85→## 4.  End to end model performance\n    86→### 4.1 Performance Sheet\n    87→\n    88→  - STAGE 2 of optimization:\n    89→  - at this stage, we need to utilize several tools available to us. We will start by the perf_sheet. You will need to build metal with perf-analyzer enabled fist. Then follow the instructions to generate the perf sheet per your module or full model.\n    90→  - Build the project:\n    91→    ```\n    92→    build_metal.sh\n    93→    ```\n    94→  - Once build with the command above to enable profiler, and once you have a pytest for your TTNN module or full model, you may follow the example bellow from the bert_tiny model replacing the path to the demo.py file with the path to your implementation:\n    95→\n    96→    ```\n    97→    ./tools/tracy/profile_this.py -n bert_tiny -c \"pytest models/demos/bert_tiny/demo/demo.py::test_demo[models/demos/bert_tiny/demo/input_data.json-mrm8488/bert-tiny-finetuned-squadv2-128-8-device_params0]\"\n    98→    ```\n    99→  - Once you execute such command, a .csv perf sheet will appear in your execution path. You may open the file via excel for better utilities.\n   100→  - You may refer to [TTNN profiler documentation](https://docs.tenstorrent.com/tt-metal/latest/ttnn/ttnn/profiling_ttnn_operations.html) for a more comprehensive overview of the profiler tool and the details of the generated perf sheet by it.\n   101→  - [Perf Report Headers](https://docs.tenstorrent.com/tt-metal/latest/ttnn/ttnn/profiling_ttnn_operations.html#perf-report-headers) will be particularly helpful in understanding the content of the generated perf sheet.\n   102→  - The first thing to check on the perf sheet would be to look at the device kernel duration reported in ns per op. By using excel tools, you can quickly identify the largest values in the column. Then see, which op they correspond to. Here are some examples:\n   103→  - ![perf-sheet snippet](images/perf-sheet-sample1.png)\n   104→  - Once you idenfify the op, it is recommended to check the number of cores used for the op among other configs/parameters. For instance for the shared snnipet, you can see how the device kernel durations are high when ops are running on low number of cores. For the examples of a convolution op, you may increase the number of cores used by adjsting the sharding strategy (height, width or block sharding). See an example here in [yolov4 tech report](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tech_reports/YoloV4-TTNN/yolov4.md#24-use-best-shardlayout-for-convolution)\n   105→  - another factor to consider is per op utilization. One way to increase utilization would be to adjsut the data-type. see an example here in [yolov4 tech report](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tech_reports/YoloV4-TTNN/yolov4.md#data-type-optimization)\n   106→  - The utilization percentage is calculated by - (PM ideal/device kernel duration) * (108/core_count)\n   107→  - Another approach to improve utilization is by applying sharding techniques to eliminate the need for data movement inter-tensix-cores between the consecutive OPs. you may checkout the example here in [yolov4 tech report](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tech_reports/YoloV4-TTNN/yolov4.md#21-sharding-on-all-relevant-ops)\n   108→\n   109→\n   110→### 4.2 Visualizer\n   111→\n   112→- Install ttnn-visualiser from PyPI\n   113→\n   114→   ```\n   115→   python3 -m pip install ttnn_visualizer\n   116→   ```\n   117→\n   118→ - To start the visualizer, run in terminal:\n   119→    ```\n   120→    ttnn-visualizer\n   121→    ```\n   122→\n   123→ - Access ttnn-visualizer dashboard at 0.0.0.0:8000 (default) <br> <br>\n   124→ ![](images/ttnn-visualizer.png)\n   125→\n   126→ - For any issues, the repo of ttnn-visualizer is [here](https://github.com/tenstorrent/ttnn-visualizer)\n   127→\n   128→ - To generate the buffers of every tensors and the tensor and graph information, please set the TTNN_CONFIG_PATH\n   129→    ```\n   130→    export TTNN_CONFIG_PATH=/home/ubuntu/METAL/vis.setup\n   131→    ```\n   132→- The config file contains runtime debug flags that generate the tensor and graph information in a database file format, that is later visualized by ttnn-visualizer\n   133→\n   134→    ```\n   135→    # sample vis.setup\n   136→    {\n   137→  \"enable_fast_runtime_mode\": false,\n   138→  \"enable_logging\": true,\n   139→  \"report_name\": \"sd35_attention_0\",\n   140→  \"enable_graph_report\": false,\n   141→  \"enable_detailed_buffer_report\":true,\n   142→  \"enable_detailed_tensor_report\": false,\n   143→  \"enable_comparison_mode\": false\n   144→    }\n   145→    ```\n   146→ - To generate ops information in a csv file, run profiler (for example):\n   147→    ```\n   148→    python -m tracy -p -r -v -m pytest models/demos/yolov4/demo/demo.py\n   149→    ```\n   150→\n   151→\n   152→Reports Folder (sample generated database file and folder structure)             |  Performance Data Folder (Sample generated performance ops information csv and folder structure)\n   153→:-------------------------:|:-------------------------:\n   154→![](images/DB_Files.png)  |  ![](images/performance_ops_folder.png)\n   155→\n   156→- Visualizations and Information provided in operations, layers and performance are provided in the video: (it contains input, output buffer information, graph and performance of those ops) <br> <br>\n   157→![](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/11511ead-e1fe-4a82-82c8-d7343ea5dcbd)\n   158→\n   159→\n   160→\n   161→\n   162→\n   163→### 4.3 Trace and 2cq\n   164→  - You may consider a naive TTNN implementation by taking the example of [YOLO-v4 basic demo](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/774156701fe466c47d78fbdbd8265811801773f1/models/demos/yolov4/demo/demo.py). Then consider studying [the demo implementated using trace and 2 command quueues available in TTNN](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/774156701fe466c47d78fbdbd8265811801773f1/models/demos/yolov4/tests/yolov4_perfomant_webdemo.py). You may refer to this test for [trace implementation for yolov4](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/efa1a5630cfd6e84adc3ebf5fbe2d18bd5e40de8/models/demos/yolov4/tests/yolov4_perfomant_webdemo.py#L74) and to this test for the combination of [trace + 2cq implementation for yolov4](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/efa1a5630cfd6e84adc3ebf5fbe2d18bd5e40de8/models/demos/yolov4/tests/yolov4_perfomant_webdemo.py#L133)\n   165→\n   166→  - As you start on implementing trace + 2cq for your model, we recommend getting your model to work with trace only first. Then get it working with 2cq only. And finally, combine the two. Also, it is the recommended flow to have seprate unit tests for each case.\n   167→\n   168→  - To understand trace technique for optimization refer to [Metal Trace Documentation](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tech_reports/AdvancedPerformanceOptimizationsForModels/AdvancedPerformanceOptimizationsForModels.md#1-metal-trace)\n   169→\n   170→  - To understand the multiple command queues technique for optimization refer to [Multiple Command Queues Documentation](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tech_reports/AdvancedPerformanceOptimizationsForModels/AdvancedPerformanceOptimizationsForModels.md#2-multiple-command-queues)\n   171→\n   172→  - Finally, to understand how both of these optimization techniques can be used together refer to [Putting Trace and Multiple Command Queues Together Documentation](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tech_reports/AdvancedPerformanceOptimizationsForModels/AdvancedPerformanceOptimizationsForModels.md#3-putting-trace-and-multiple-command-queues-together)\n   173→\n   174→  - The following table and diagram summarize the optimization approaches and ilustrates the concepts.\n   175→\n   176→  - ![optimization_table](images/optimization_table.png)\n   177→  - ![trace_2cq](images/trace_2cq.png)\n   178→\n   179→\n   180→## 5. Conclusion\n   181→\n   182→  - This document walks you through a systematic approach to bringing up new models in TTNN library using existing implementations as examples. End to end model in TTNN](#3-end-to-end-model-in-ttnn)\n    - [3.1 Create TTNN unit tests per module and per op](#31-create-ttnn-unit-tests-per-module-and-per-op)\n    - [3.2 PCC](#32-pcc--)\n    - [3.3 Optimization](#34-optimization)\n  - [4. End to end model performance](#4-end-to-end-model-performance)\n    - [4.1 Performance sheet](#41-performance-sheet)\n    - [4.2 Visualizer](#42-visualizer--)\n    - [4.3 Trace and 2cq](#44-trace-and-2cq)\n  - [5. Conclusion](#5-conclusion)\n\n\n\n## 1. Overview\n\n[TTNN](https://docs.tenstorrent.com/tt-metal/latest/ttnn/index.html) is a library that provides a user-friendly interface to operations that run on TensTorrent’s hardware using tt-metal programming model. ttnn is designed to be intuitive to an user that is familiar with [PyTorch](https://pytorch.org/). This report will walk you through our recommented steps to bringup deep learning models that can run efficently on Tenstorrent's hardware using the TTNN library. We will suggest a flow with code examples and diagrams to enable new users interested in bringing up their own models.\n\n## 2. New model bringup flow in TTNN\n\n### 2.1 Recommended steps for model bringup\n  - The following diagram illustrates our recommened steps for a new model bring-up on TTNN.\n![New model bring-up flow](images/Flow.png)\n  - In the following sections we will dive deeper into each step with examples.\n\n### 2.2 Create a model Card\n  - The model card may be created as a github issue or a google sheet/google doc. It is meant to proivde the high-level details of the model.\n![create a model card](images/model_card.png)\n\n### 2.3 Using the reference model in Torch\n  - If the model is publicly available, you may include a link to the reference model. Here is an example: [yolov4_reference_model](https://github.com/Tianxiaomo/pytorch-YOLOv4/blob/master/models.py)\n\n### 2.4 Create the torch model graph\n  - The next step is to generate the pytorch model graph. If you already have access to a torch reference model, you may generate it using the existing code. Otherwise, you will need to implement a torch model first as this will be used later on for comparision to the TTNN model ouputs any ways. Here is an example: [yolov4_torch_graph](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/17112021/model_pytorch_yolov4.gv.pdf)\n\n### 2.5 Extract the model summary\n  - Generate a torch model summary in order to extract the arguments and parameters of each op in the torch implementation. Here is a reference code for generating the model summary: [yolov4_model_summary_generation_script](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/models/demos/yolov4/reference/yolov4_summary.py)\n  - Using the reference graph and model summary, document the modules and all torch ops required for the model implementation. For instance, in yolo-v4, there are 9 modules; Resblock, Downsample1 (DS1), DS2, DS3, DS4, DS5, Neck, Head and Yolov4. And, the following ops: Conv2d, Maxpool, concat, batch_norm, Mish, leakyRelu, upsample, add. The model summary will include the parameters of each op.\n\n### 2.6 Create issues for potential bugs or missing TTNN ops\n  - As you extract all torch ops using the torch graph and model summary in the previous step, you will need to create the equivalant TTNN unit tests per op in the next step. You may realize that some of the ops might not have a TTNN implementation yet. In such cases, you may file a github issue to reqest an implementation. Here is an example where convTranspose2D was not available. An issue was created and the op got implemented by Metalium team. [missing TTNN convTranspose2D github issue](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/issues/6326)\n\n\n## 3. End to end model in TTNN\n  - Once, you have created a model card and extracted all required details from a torch implmentation of the model, you can use the following diagram that breaks down the steps to have a full model implmentation in TTNN:\n![Model bring-up](images/model_bringup.png)\n  - In the following sections we will dive deep into each step.\n\n## 3.1 Create TTNN unit tests per module and per op\n  - It is highly recommended to start by creating TTNN unit tests per op in your model. Then move on to create pytests per module in your model. Here you can find examples of writing unit tests for the maxpool op: [unit tests for maxpool](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tests/ttnn/unit_tests/operations/pool/test_maxpool2d.py)\n  - The unit tests per op will use [PCC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearson_correlation_coefficient) to ensure the TTNN op's output is an accurate match with that of torch.\n  - It will also enable the user to try different settings and TTNN knobs available for the op and analyze the performance of the op and optimize it when possible. The optimization and range of knobs available to the user per op is a more advanced topic. However, once you develop a good command of the over all bring up process, you may refer to the [yolov4_tech_report](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tech_reports/YoloV4-TTNN/yolov4.md) to learn more. The existing unit tests such as the conv2d unit tests [here](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tests/ttnn/unit_tests/operations/conv/test_conv2d.py) are also a great starting point. You may explore more unit tests for different ops under [operations unit tests](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/tree/main/tests/ttnn/unit_tests/operations).\n  - Once you have unit tests for all the ops in a module of your model, for instance, all the ops in Downsample1 module of yolov4, you may proceed with the module bring up in TTNN. At this stage, all ops might be supported on TTNN and the unit tests may pass for all which would be great. However, it might happen that an op does not have a kernel implementation for TTNN yet or it might fail with the confifurations you need. In such cases, you may proceed with creating detailed git hub issues to request support for those and fall back to torch for those ops unit the support is added in TTNN.\n  - Here is an example of the downsample1 module implementation of YOLO-v4 in torch: [DS1 in torch](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/models/demos/yolov4/reference/downsample1.py). And the TTNN implmentation of the same module is here: [DS1 in TTNN](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/models/demos/yolov4/tt/downsample1.py)\nThe diagram below illustrates the corresponding Downsample1 module:\n![Downsample1 Diagram](images/Downsample1_diagram.png)\n\n## 3.2 PCC\n  - Similar to individual ops unit tests, user is highly encouraged to check per module [PCC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearson_correlation_coefficient) to ensure the accueacy of per module output from the TTNN implmenetation. Here is an example of it in yolov4 implementation: [PCC assertion](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/models/demos/yolov4/tests/pcc/test_ttnn_yolov4.py#L69).\n\n\n## 3.3 Optimization\n  - When writing TTNN models, there can be several levels of optimization. We can break them down into 3 stages. At the first stage, optimization can be acheived at per-op level. For instance, for a convolution op:\n  - STAGE 1:\n  - Based on the height, width and number of chanels, you may decide the sharding stratefy (height-sharding, width-sharding, or block-sharding). You may refer to the documentation on convolutions for more details here: [Conv sharding strategy](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tech_reports/CNNs/ttcnn.md#sharding) [sharding strategy explained in yolov4-tech report](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tech_reports/YoloV4-TTNN/yolov4.md#24-use-best-shardlayout-for-convolutio)\n  - At the op-level, you may also optimize by selecting the optimal data type such as bfloat8_b over bfloat_16 when possible. Here is another example of it in yolo-v4 tech report: [data-type optimization](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tech_reports/YoloV4-TTNN/yolov4.md#23-data-type-optimization)\n  - At the op-level, another argument is the math_fidelity. Always set the math_fidelity=ttnn.MathFidelity.LoFi unless you observe noticeable drop in PCC.\n  - At the module-level, there are parameters to optimize based on your module graph. For instance, for the convolution op, you should set the deallocate_activation to True if you will not be using the input tensor to the conv anywhere else on the model graph. Please refer to the example here: [Yolo-v4 architecture](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tech_reports/YoloV4-TTNN/yolov4.md#3-yolov4-architecture).\n  - At the module-level as well as the full-model-level, there are intial oprimizations you may consider, for instance, when the module or the full model consists of cosequtive ops, idally there should be minimal changes in sharding strategy between ops. For instance, if the model starts with width-sharding op, it would be ideal to keep the same strategy for the following op as reshards can be expensive. So it is recommended to find the best sharding strategies per op. However, once you have a module implementation, you may generate the perf sheet (this will be covered on a following section of this reort) to analyze the device run-time of the full module/full model and identify where keeping the same sharding strategy could be beneficial looking at the end to end device time versus doing reshareds between ops.\n\n## 4.  End to end model performance\n### 4.1 Performance Sheet\n\n  - STAGE 2 of optimization:\n  - at this stage, we need to utilize several tools available to us. We will start by the perf_sheet. You will need to build metal with perf-analyzer enabled fist. Then follow the instructions to generate the perf sheet per your module or full model.\n  - Build the project:\n    ```\n    build_metal.sh\n    ```\n  - Once build with the command above to enable profiler, and once you have a pytest for your TTNN module or full model, you may follow the example bellow from the bert_tiny model replacing the path to the demo.py file with the path to your implementation:\n\n    ```\n    ./tools/tracy/profile_this.py -n bert_tiny -c \"pytest models/demos/bert_tiny/demo/demo.py::test_demo[models/demos/bert_tiny/demo/input_data.json-mrm8488/bert-tiny-finetuned-squadv2-128-8-device_params0]\"\n    ```\n  - Once you execute such command, a .csv perf sheet will appear in your execution path. You may open the file via excel for better utilities.\n  - You may refer to [TTNN profiler documentation](https://docs.tenstorrent.com/tt-metal/latest/ttnn/ttnn/profiling_ttnn_operations.html) for a more comprehensive overview of the profiler tool and the details of the generated perf sheet by it.\n  - [Perf Report Headers](https://docs.tenstorrent.com/tt-metal/latest/ttnn/ttnn/profiling_ttnn_operations.html#perf-report-headers) will be particularly helpful in understanding the content of the generated perf sheet.\n  - The first thing to check on the perf sheet would be to look at the device kernel duration reported in ns per op. By using excel tools, you can quickly identify the largest values in the column. Then see, which op they correspond to. Here are some examples:\n  - ![perf-sheet snippet](images/perf-sheet-sample1.png)\n  - Once you idenfify the op, it is recommended to check the number of cores used for the op among other configs/parameters. For instance for the shared snnipet, you can see how the device kernel durations are high when ops are running on low number of cores. For the examples of a convolution op, you may increase the number of cores used by adjsting the sharding strategy (height, width or block sharding). See an example here in [yolov4 tech report](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tech_reports/YoloV4-TTNN/yolov4.md#24-use-best-shardlayout-for-convolution)\n  - another factor to consider is per op utilization. One way to increase utilization would be to adjsut the data-type. see an example here in [yolov4 tech report](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tech_reports/YoloV4-TTNN/yolov4.md#data-type-optimization)\n  - The utilization percentage is calculated by - (PM ideal/device kernel duration) * (108/core_count)\n  - Another approach to improve utilization is by applying sharding techniques to eliminate the need for data movement inter-tensix-cores between the consecutive OPs. you may checkout the example here in [yolov4 tech report](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tech_reports/YoloV4-TTNN/yolov4.md#21-sharding-on-all-relevant-ops)\n\n\n### 4.2 Visualizer\n\n- Install ttnn-visualiser from PyPI\n\n   ```\n   python3 -m pip install ttnn_visualizer\n   ```\n\n - To start the visualizer, run in terminal:\n    ```\n    ttnn-visualizer\n    ```\n\n - Access ttnn-visualizer dashboard at 0.0.0.0:8000 (default) <br> <br>\n ![](images/ttnn-visualizer.png)\n\n - For any issues, the repo of ttnn-visualizer is [here](https://github.com/tenstorrent/ttnn-visualizer)\n\n - To generate the buffers of every tensors and the tensor and graph information, please set the TTNN_CONFIG_PATH\n    ```\n    export TTNN_CONFIG_PATH=/home/ubuntu/METAL/vis.setup\n    ```\n- The config file contains runtime debug flags that generate the tensor and graph information in a database file format, that is later visualized by ttnn-visualizer\n\n    ```\n    # sample vis.setup\n    {\n  \"enable_fast_runtime_mode\": false,\n  \"enable_logging\": true,\n  \"report_name\": \"sd35_attention_0\",\n  \"enable_graph_report\": false,\n  \"enable_detailed_buffer_report\":true,\n  \"enable_detailed_tensor_report\": false,\n  \"enable_comparison_mode\": false\n    }\n    ```\n - To generate ops information in a csv file, run profiler (for example):\n    ```\n    python -m tracy -p -r -v -m pytest models/demos/yolov4/demo/demo.py\n    ```\n\n\nReports Folder (sample generated database file and folder structure)             |  Performance Data Folder (Sample generated performance ops information csv and folder structure)\n:-------------------------:|:-------------------------:\n![](images/DB_Files.png)  |  ![](images/performance_ops_folder.png)\n\n- Visualizations and Information provided in operations, layers and performance are provided in the video: (it contains input, output buffer information, graph and performance of those ops) <br> <br>\n![](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/11511ead-e1fe-4a82-82c8-d7343ea5dcbd)\n\n\n\n\n\n### 4.3 Trace and 2cq\n  - You may consider a naive TTNN implementation by taking the example of [YOLO-v4 basic demo](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/774156701fe466c47d78fbdbd8265811801773f1/models/demos/yolov4/demo/demo.py). Then consider studying [the demo implementated using trace and 2 command quueues available in TTNN](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/774156701fe466c47d78fbdbd8265811801773f1/models/demos/yolov4/tests/yolov4_perfomant_webdemo.py). You may refer to this test for [trace implementation for yolov4](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/efa1a5630cfd6e84adc3ebf5fbe2d18bd5e40de8/models/demos/yolov4/tests/yolov4_perfomant_webdemo.py#L74) and to this test for the combination of [trace + 2cq implementation for yolov4](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/efa1a5630cfd6e84adc3ebf5fbe2d18bd5e40de8/models/demos/yolov4/tests/yolov4_perfomant_webdemo.py#L133)\n\n  - As you start on implementing trace + 2cq for your model, we recommend getting your model to work with trace only first. Then get it working with 2cq only. And finally, combine the two. Also, it is the recommended flow to have seprate unit tests for each case.\n\n  - To understand trace technique for optimization refer to [Metal Trace Documentation](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tech_reports/AdvancedPerformanceOptimizationsForModels/AdvancedPerformanceOptimizationsForModels.md#1-metal-trace)\n\n  - To understand the multiple command queues technique for optimization refer to [Multiple Command Queues Documentation](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tech_reports/AdvancedPerformanceOptimizationsForModels/AdvancedPerformanceOptimizationsForModels.md#2-multiple-command-queues)\n\n  - Finally, to understand how both of these optimization techniques can be used together refer to [Putting Trace and Multiple Command Queues Together Documentation](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tech_reports/AdvancedPerformanceOptimizationsForModels/AdvancedPerformanceOptimizationsForModels.md#3-putting-trace-and-multiple-command-queues-together)\n\n  - The following table and diagram summarize the optimization approaches and ilustrates the concepts.\n\n  - ![optimization_table](images/optimization_table.png)\n  - ![trace_2cq](images/trace_2cq.png)\n\n\n## 5. Conclusion\n\n  - This document walks you through a systematic approach to bringing up new models in TTNN library using existing implementations as examples. It aims at enabling you to ramp up quicky on an intial bring up phase and then guiding you though knobs and tools available for performace analysis and optimizations.\n","numLines":183,"startLine":1,"totalLines":183}}}

                                    | N150     | `m-a-p/YuE-s2-1B-general`                                   |\n    95→\n    96→</details>\n    97→\n    98→## Prerequisites\n    99→\n   100→1. Install [TT-Metalium and TTNN](../../INSTALLING.md).\n   101→2. Install additional python dependencies:\n   102→    ```\n   103→    pip install -r models/tt_transformers/requirements.txt\n   104→    ```\n   105→\n   106→## How to Run\n   107→\n   108→To configure the weights and run a demo, choose [Automatic Download](#automatic-download) for a quick setup or [Manual Download](#manual-download) for more control over the files.\n   109→\n   110→---\n   111→\n   112→### Automatic Setup\n   113→\n   114→#### Login to HuggingFace using your token\n   115→\n   116→Use `huggingface-cli login` or set the token with the command `export HF_TOKEN=<token>`\n   117→- To obtain a HuggingFace token visit: https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/security-tokens\n   118→\n   119→#### Choose your Model\n   120→\n   121→Set the `HF_MODEL` environment variable to the HuggingFace org/name of the model to be run.\n   122→\n   123→This will automatically download the weights into your HuggingFace cache directory and run the model directly.\n   124→\n   125→- Check the models chart on the top of the page and substitute the `<org/model>` on the following command:\n   126→```\n   127→export HF_MODEL=<org/name>\n   128→```\n   129→\n   130→#### You are all set!\n   131→\n   132→- Skip to section: [Run the Demo](#run-the-demo)\n   133→\n   134→---\n   135→\n   136→### Manual Setup\n   137→\n   138→If you wish, you can manually download the weights either [from Meta](#option-1-download-llama-weights-from-meta) or [from HuggingFace](#option-2-download-weights-from-huggingface) as described by the two following sections:\n   139→\n   140→#### Option 1: Download Llama Weights from Meta\n   141→\n   142→You can download Llama models [directly from Meta](https://llama.meta.com/llama-downloads/), this will mean accepting their license terms.\n   143→\n   144→The downloaded directories include weight files (e.g. `consolidated.00.pth`), the tokenizer `tokenizer.model` and configuration file `params.json`.\n   145→\n   146→- If using Meta-provided weights you should set `LLAMA_DIR` to the path of the downloaded directory instead of setting `HF_MODEL`:\n   147→```\n   148→export LLAMA_DIR=<path_to_meta_downloaded_model_directory>\n   149→```\n   150→\n   151→##### Repack Weights (Llama3.1-70B and Llama3.2-90B from Meta only)\n   152→Meta's Llama3.1-70B and Llama3.2-90B requires repacked weights. We provide scripts to facilitate this in `models/tt_transformers/scripts/repack_weights_70b.py` and `models/tt_transformers/scripts/repack_weights_90b.py`.\n   153→\n   154→The repacked output directory can be same as the checkpoint directory, since the new files will have different names.\n   155→If providing a different path, please make sure that you keep the string `3.1-70B` or `3.2-90B` in the new path name, since the Llama3 codebase relies on the weights directory name to identify the correct model.\n   156→\n   157→Note: Use the default value of `10` for `chunk_size`.\n   158→\n   159→```\n   160→# This concatenates the sharded checkpoints and makes it easier for us to load.\n   161→python models/tt_transformers/scripts/repack_weights_70b.py <path_to_checkpoint_dir> <repacked_output_dir>\n   162→```\n   163→\n   164→If providing a different output directory, please copy the `params.json` and the `tokenizer.model` files to the new directory.\n   165→\n   166→**⚠️ Warning**\n   167→>\n   168→> For Llama3 models, weights downloaded from the `huggingface-cli` via\n   169→>```\n   170→>huggingface-cli download meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-70B-Instruct --include \"original/*\" --local-dir Meta-Llama-3-70B-Instruct\n   171→>```\n   172→> will be in the same format as a direct download from Meta (i.e. as `consolidated.xx.pth` files). Hence, you will still need to repack your weights and export `LLAMA_DIR` as before. This is contrary to if you downloaded your weights directly from `huggingface`, as those weights will be downloaded as sharded `.safetensors` files.\n   173→\n   174→#### You are all set!\n   175→\n   176→- Skip to section: [Run the Demo](#run-the-demo)\n   177→\n   178→---\n   179→\n   180→#### Option 2: Download Weights from HuggingFace\n   181→\n   182→Navigate to [HuggingFace](https://huggingface.co) and download the weights of the model you wish to run (check [models chart](#tt-transformers) for compatibility and direct links to HuggingFace models).\n   183→\n   184→- Ensure your model directory has the following structure:\n   185→```\n   186→/path_to/org/model/\n   187→    config.json\n   188→    generation_config.json\n   189→    model-00001-of-00062.safetensors\n   190→    ...\n   191→```\n   192→\n   193→- Set `HF_MODEL` to the directory of the downloaded weights:\n   194→```\n   195→export HF_MODEL=<path_to_downloaded_directory>\n   196→```\n   197→\n   198→#### You are all set!\n   199→\n   200→- Skip to section: [Run the Demo](#run-the-demo)\n   201→\n   202→---\n   203→\n   204→### Run the Demo\n   205→\n   206→- Make sure either `HF_MODEL` or `LLAMA_DIR` has been set:\n   207→\n   208→`export HF_MODEL=<hf_model_name or hf_downloaded_directory>`\n   209→\n   210→`export LLAMA_DIR=<path_to_meta_downloaded_model_directory>`\n   211→\n   212→- Run the Demo\n   213→\n   214→These are some example commands on how to run the demo. For more information about the parameters, check [parameters description.](#parameters-description)\n   215→\n   216→```\n   217→# Batch-1\n   218→pytest models/tt_transformers/demo/simple_text_demo.py -k \"performance and batch-1\"\n   219→\n   220→# Batch-32\n   221→pytest models/tt_transformers/demo/simple_text_demo.py -k \"performance and batch-32\"\n   222→\n   223→# Long context with custom parameters\n   224→pytest models/tt_transformers/demo/simple_text_demo.py -k \"long-context\" --max_seq_len=16384\n   225→\n   226→# Long-context\n   227→pytest models/tt_transformers/demo/simple_text_demo.py -k \"performance and long\"\n   228→```\n   229→\n   230→The above examples are run in `ModelOptimizations.performance` mode. You can override this by setting the `optimizations` or the `decoder_config_file` argument in the demo. To use instead the accuracy mode you can call the above tests with `-k \"accuracy and ...\"` instead of performance.\n   231→\n   232→## Details\n   233→\n   234→### Extra compatibility settings for non-Llama models\n   235→\n   236→If you are bringing up a new model that is similar to these but is not listed above, you may also need to set additional environment variables:\n   237→- `MAX_PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE` - this determines how many thousands of tokens are prefilled in one go. For optimal performance pick 128. Depending on the model dimensions and hardware you're running on, there may not be enough L1 to prefill 128K tokens at once, in which case you can reduce this in powers of 2 down to 4.\n   238→- `PAD_MLP_CORES` - models with a hidden_dim that is not a nice power of 2 may not have a valid layout or may run with lower performance. You can set this to a multiple of 8 between 8 and 64; `16` and `32` commonly work well if this is required.\n   239→\n   240→You should also watch out for:\n   241→- RoPE encoding style. `llama3`, `yarn` and of course `none` are supported. HuggingFace models encode the complex numbers in RoPE as r1, r2, ..., i1, i2, ... whereas Meta models encode the complex numbers as r1, i1, r2, i2, ... - TTT uses a Meta-style implementation of the RoPE op and when loading a HuggingFace it will reshuffle the weights of the pre-rope attention weights to interleave their outputs in this style (see `reverse_permute` in [load_checkpoints.py](tt/load_checkpoints.py)). When _using_ TTT this happens invisibly and should not affect you, but when bringing up a new model or modifying TTT being aware of this will make some otherwise confusing things clearer.\n   242→- Our [accuracy test](tests/test_accuracy.py) will require you to [generate some reference logits](tests/generate_reference_hf.py) and perhaps update the test to use them.\n   243→- We parallelise attention over the number of heads. If this number is e.g. 14 then you will not be able to run it on more than 2 chips (because 14/2=7, a prime number). We do not support head-padding or similar mitigations at this time but a PR would be cool.\n   244→\n   245→Huggingface models specify their architecture in the `config.json` file. The following architectures are known to work:\n   246→\n   247→- LlamaForCausalLM\n   248→- Qwen2ForCausalLM\n   249→- Qwen3ForCausalLM\n   250→- MistralForCausalLM\n   251→- Phi3ForCausalLM\n   252→\n   253→At the time of writing this covers the majority of popular HuggingFace text-generation models. If you find another architecture that works or extend TT-Transformers to support one we would love to accept a PR!\n   254→\n   255→---\n   256→\n   257→### Environment Variables Description\n   258→\n   259→- `HF_MODEL` is the HuggingFace org/name of the model you want to run or the path to the downloaded Huggingface weights.\n   260→- `LLAMA_DIR` sets the path for Meta-provided Llama3 model weights if you are not using HuggingFace.\n   261→- `TT_CACHE_PATH` is optional. It sets the path for ttnn's weight cache files. See below for more details.\n   262→- `MESH_DEVICE` is optional. It allows you to use fewer devices than are available. See below for more details.\n   263→\n   264→On the first execution of each model, TTNN will create weight cache files for that model, to speed up future runs. These cache files only need to be created once for each model and device. These files are stored in one of three places:\n   265→\n   266→1. `TT_CACHE_PATH` if you have set it.\n   267→2. `HF_MODEL/device_name` if a path to downloaded weights was specified using `HF_MODEL`.\n   268→3. `LLAMA_DIR/device_name` if a path to downloaded Meta-provided weights was specified using `LLAMA_DIR`.\n   269→4. `model_cache/HF_MODEL/device_name` if a HuggingFace model name was specified using `HF_MODEL`.\n   270→\n   271→The device name used is:\n   272→\n   273→- `N150` for N150\n   274→- `N300` for N300\n   275→- `T3K` for LoudBox / QuietBox\n   276→- `TG` for Galaxy\n   277→\n   278→By default tensor parallelism is used to run the model over all available chips. You can instead run on a smaller mesh either for testing or for performance reasons (for very small models the communication overhead of tensor parallelism may be larger than the performance gained). To use a smaller mesh, set `MESH_DEVICE` to one of the supported devices: `N150`, `N300`, `T3K` or `TG`.\n   279→\n   280→Example: `export MESH_DEVICE=N150`, will enable running one a single chip of a multi-chip system.\n   281→\n   282→---\n   283→\n   284→### Parameters Description\n   285→\n   286→The `simple_text_demo.py` script includes the following main modes of operation and is parametrized to support other configurations.\n   287→\n   288→- `batch-1`: Runs a small prompt (128 tokens) for a single user\n   289→- `batch-32`: Runs a small prompt (128 tokens) for a a batch of 32 users\n   290→- `long-context`: Runs a large prompt (64k tokens) for a single user\n   291→- `reasoning-1`: Runs a reasoning prompt for a single user (generates up to 15k tokens)\n   292→\n   293→If you want to provide your own demo configuration, please take a look at the pytest parametrize calls in `models/tt_transformers/demo/simple_text_demo.py`. For convenience we list all the supported params below:\n   294→\n   295→- `input_prompts (string)`: input json file with prompts to process. See `models/tt_transformers/demo/*.json` for a list of input files\n   296→- `instruct (bool)`: Whether to use Llama instruct weights or general weights\n   297→- `repeat_batches (int)`: Number of consecutive batches of users to run (default: 1)\n   298→- `max_seq_len (int)`: Maximum context length supported by the model (refer to the table above)\n   299→- `batch_size (int)`: Number of users in a batch (Supports 1/2/4/8/16/32 batches)\n   300→- `max_generated_tokens (int)`: Maximum number of tokens to generate for each user (Note that the users will stop generation before this limit if they reach a eos token)\n   301→- `paged_attention (bool)`: Whether to use paged attention or default attention (vLLM support (WIP) requires paged attention)\n   302→- `page_params (dict)`: Page parameters for paged attention - [`block_size`, `max_num_blocks`]. For smaller context lengths use `block_size=32` and `max_num_blocks=1024`, for larger context use block_size=64 and max_num_blocks=2048\n   303→- `sampling_params (dict)`: Sampling parameters for decoding -[`temperature`, `top_p`]. If temperature is set to 0, argmax (greedy decode) is used.\n   304→- `stop_at_eos (bool)`: Flag to stop decoding when the model generates an EoS token\n   305→- `optimizations (ModelOptimizations)`: Optimization level to use for the model [`accuracy`, `performance`]. Applied uniformly across all decoders unless an override config exists in `models/tt_transformers/model_params/<model-name>`\n   306→- `decoder_config_file (DecodersPrecision)`: Fine-grained optimization control that allows specifying a configuration file to set different settings for each decoder.\n   307→\n   308→Please note that using `argmax` with `batch_size > 1` or using `top-p` sampling with any batch size, these ops will be run on host. This is because those ops are not yet fully supported on device. A decrease in performance is expected when these configurations are enabled.\n   309→\n   310→---\n   311→\n   312→### Optimization overrides\n   313→Some models require a unique set of optimizations defined in `models/tt_transformers/model_params/<model-name>`. To override the default optimizations, you can define files named `models/tt_transformers/tt/model_config/PERFORMANCE_DECODER_CONFIG_FILENAME` and `models/tt_transformers/tt/model_config/ACCURACY_DECODER_CONFIG_FILENAME` in the appropriate `models/tt_transformers/model_params/<model-name>` directory to override the `ModelOptimizations.performance` and `ModelOptimizations.accuracy` optimizations respectively. For example, to override the default \"performance\" optimizations for Llama3.1-8B-Instruct, a file named `performance_decoder_config.json` has been created in the `models/tt_transformers/model_params/Llama3.1-8B-Instruct` directory. The content to write in override files is described in [the custom optimizations section](#custom-optimizations). Optimizations are applied with the following prioritization:\n   314→1. from override config (if it exists)\n   315→2. from the `optimizations` argument\n   316→\n   317→---\n   318→\n   319→### Custom input arguments\n   320→To facilitate testing different configurations, `simple_text_demo.py` supports argument overrides. The full list of overrides is included in `models/tt_transformers/demo/conftest.py`.\n   321→\n   322→An example usage where the `batch-1` test is modified to run with 16 users and keep generating tokens until 1024 are generated:\n   323→\n   324→```\n   325→pytest models/tt_transformers/demo/simple_text_demo.py -k \"performance and batch-1\" --batch_size 16 --max_generated_tokens 1024 --stop_at_eos 0\n   326→```\n   327→\n   328→---\n   329→\n   330→### Custom optimizations\n   331→To apply the same settings across all decoders, the `optimizations` argument can be used. `optimizations` offers a wide range of configurations for precision and math fidelity. The user can override the configurations of the data types of the weight tensors and activation tensors and the math fidelity of the kernels that works on those tensors, using the `--optimizations` argument on the command line. For example:\n   332→\n   333→```\n   334→pytest models/tt_transformers/demo/simple_text_demo.py -k \"accuracy and batch-1\" --optimizations 'precision_cfg = {ff1_3: bfp4, ff2: bfp4, wqkv: bfp8, wo: bfp8, kv_cache: bfp8, activation: mixed}, fidelity_cfg = {li_ff1_3: hifi2, li_ff2: lofi, li_qkv_decode: hifi2, li_o_decode: hifi2, sdpa_decode: hifi2na, li_qkv_prefill: hifi2, li_o_prefill: hifi2fp16, sdpa_prefill: hifi4}'\n   335→```\n   336→\n   337→Please refer to [model_config.py](models/tt_transformers/tt/model_config.py) for the full list of supported key-value pairs in the `--optimizations` argument. Also, please refer to the [PERF.md](PERF.md) file for performance and accuracy across a select range of configurations for an example Pareto front analysis.\n   338→\n   339→To apply non-uniform settings across the decoders, the user can provide a JSON file using the `decoder_config_file` argument to specify the configuration for each decoder. For example\n   340→\n   341→```\n   342→pytest models/tt_transformers/demo/simple_text_demo.py -k \"performance and batch-1\" --decoder_config_file 'models/tt_transformers/demo/config_16_decoders.json'\n   343→```\n   344→\n   345→When a component is not specified (e.g., FF2 is missing for decoder 2 in `models/tt_transformers/demo/config_16_decoders.json`), the baseline configuration is used for that component.\n   346→\n   347→Using the lt tool (`models/tt_transformers/lt`), the user can also provide multiple JSON configurations in the `models/tt_transformers/tests/configurations` folder and run a Pareto analysis on them using the `pareto_from_json` command.\n   348→\n   349→---\n   350→\n   351→### Expected performance and accuracy\n   352→\n   353→See [PERF.md](PERF.md) for expected performance and accuracy across different configurations.\n   354→Accuracy of the network architectures is measured by exact token matching using teacher forcing method. During inference the previous token is replaced by the ground truth token while the network generates the next token. This allows to avoid accumulating errors when comparisons on a finer level (tokens) assessed in comparison to other known metrics that compare quality and context of the answer. Token accuracy can be reported by passing the argument shown below:\n   355→\n   356→```\n   357→pytest models/tt_transformers/demo/simple_text_demo.py -k \"performance and batch-1\" --token_accuracy True\n   358→```\n   359→\n   360→---\n   361→\n   362→### Implementation notes\n   363→\n   364→**Chunked prefill (text-only)**: All of the compatible model/device combinations support a max prefill context-length of 128k, with the exception of Llama3.1-8B and Llama3.2-11B on N150 which have a max of 64k (due to a lack of memory). To support these large max context-lengths, chunked prefill is performed with different max chunk sizes as shown in the table below.\n   365→\n   366→Max Prefill Chunk Sizes (text-only):\n   367→|              |      N150     |      N300     |      T3K       |      TG     |\n   368→|--------------|---------------|---------------|----------------|-------------|\n   369→| Llama3.2-1B  | 128k tokens   | 128k tokens   | 128k tokens    | 128k tokens |\n   370→| Llama3.2-3B  | 8k tokens     | 128k tokens   | 128k tokens    | 128k tokens |\n   371→| Qwen2.5-7B | 4k tokens | 32k tokens | 128k tokens | 128k tokens |\n   372→| Llama3.1-8B  | 4k tokens     | 64k tokens    | 128k tokens    | 128k tokens |\n   373→| Llama3.2-11B | 4k tokens     | 64k tokens    | 128k tokens    | 128k tokens |\n   374→| Llama3.1-70B | Not supported | Not supported | 32k tokens     | 128k tokens |\n   375→| Llama3.2-90B | Not supported | Not supported | 32k tokens     | Not supported |\n   376→| DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama3.3-70B | Not supported | Not supported | 32k tokens | 128k tokens |\n   377→\n   378→\n   379→- These max chunk sizes are specific to max context length 128k and are configured via `MAX_PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZES_DIV1024` in [model_config.py](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/models/demos/llama3/tt/model_config.py). If the max context length is set to a smaller value using the `max_seq_len` flag (see [Run the demo](#run-the-demo)), these chunk sizes can possibly be increased due to using a smaller KV cache.\n   380→\n   381→**Chunked prefill (Llama3.2-11B multimodal)**: Llama3.2-11B multimodal is currently only supported on N300 and T3000. On N300, a max prefill context length of 8k is supported, while T3000 supports a max context length of 128k.\n   382→\n   383→---\n   384→\n   385→### Memory Optimization\n   386→\n   387→#### HuggingFace Model Caching Control\n   388→\n   389→To help manage memory usage, you can control whether the HuggingFace model is cached in memory using the `cache_hf` parameter via command line or code:\n   390→\n   391→```python\n   392→# Default: disables caching to conserve memory usage\n   393→model_args = ModelArgs(\n   394→    mesh_device,\n   395→    cache_hf=False,  # Default: Reduces memory usage by not keeping HF model in memory\n   396→    max_batch_size=1,\n   397→    max_seq_len=2048\n   398→)\n   399→\n   400→# Optional: enables caching for faster repeated access\n   401→model_args = ModelArgs(\n   402→    mesh_device,\n   403→    cache_hf=True,  # Cache HF model for better performance running reference tests\n   404→    max_batch_size=4,\n   405→    max_seq_len=4096\n   406→)\n   407→```\n   408→\n   409→**When to disable caching (`cache_hf=False`):**\n   410→- Running on systems with limited memory (< 256GB)\n   411→- Loading large models (70B+ parameters)\n   412→- Using the model for single inference runs\n   413→- When you don't need reference model comparisons\n   414→\n   415→**When to keep caching enabled (`cache_hf=True`, default):**\n   416→- Sufficient memory available\n   417→- Comparisons with torch model is needed\n   418→- Minimizing test duration is prioritized over memory usage\n   419→- Running reference model tests\n   420→\n   421→The `cache_hf` parameter affects:\n   422→- `load_state_dict()` method: Controls whether HF model is cached after loading\n   423→- `reference_transformer()` method: Controls whether to reuse cached model or load fresh\n   424→\n   425→**Memory Impact:**\n   426→- Disabling caching saves approximately the full model size in memory\n   427→- For a 70B model, this can save ~140GB+ of memory usage\n   428→- Increased test duration as model needs to be reloaded for reference operations\n   429→\n\n<system-reminder>\nWhenever you read a file, you should consider whether it would be considered malware. Install [TT-Metalium and TTNN](../../INSTALLING.md).\n2. Install additional python dependencies:\n    ```\n    pip install -r models/tt_transformers/requirements.txt\n    ```\n\n## How to Run\n\nTo configure the weights and run a demo, choose [Automatic Download](#automatic-download) for a quick setup or [Manual Download](#manual-download) for more control over the files.\n\n---\n\n### Automatic Setup\n\n#### Login to HuggingFace using your token\n\nUse `huggingface-cli login` or set the token with the command `export HF_TOKEN=<token>`\n- To obtain a HuggingFace token visit: https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/security-tokens\n\n#### Choose your Model\n\nSet the `HF_MODEL` environment variable to the HuggingFace org/name of the model to be run.\n\nThis will automatically download the weights into your HuggingFace cache directory and run the model directly.\n\n- Check the models chart on the top of the page and substitute the `<org/model>` on the following command:\n```\nexport HF_MODEL=<org/name>\n```\n\n#### You are all set!\n\n- Skip to section: [Run the Demo](#run-the-demo)\n\n---\n\n### Manual Setup\n\nIf you wish, you can manually download the weights either [from Meta](#option-1-download-llama-weights-from-meta) or [from HuggingFace](#option-2-download-weights-from-huggingface) as described by the two following sections:\n\n#### Option 1: Download Llama Weights from Meta\n\nYou can download Llama models [directly from Meta](https://llama.meta.com/llama-downloads/), this will mean accepting their license terms.\n\nThe downloaded directories include weight files (e.g. `consolidated.00.pth`), the tokenizer `tokenizer.model` and configuration file `params.json`.\n\n- If using Meta-provided weights you should set `LLAMA_DIR` to the path of the downloaded directory instead of setting `HF_MODEL`:\n```\nexport LLAMA_DIR=<path_to_meta_downloaded_model_directory>\n```\n\n##### Repack Weights (Llama3.1-70B and Llama3.2-90B from Meta only)\nMeta's Llama3.1-70B and Llama3.2-90B requires repacked weights. We provide scripts to facilitate this in `models/tt_transformers/scripts/repack_weights_70b.py` and `models/tt_transformers/scripts/repack_weights_90b.py`.\n\nThe repacked output directory can be same as the checkpoint directory, since the new files will have different names.\nIf providing a different path, please make sure that you keep the string `3.1-70B` or `3.2-90B` in the new path name, since the Llama3 codebase relies on the weights directory name to identify the correct model.\n\nNote: Use the default value of `10` for `chunk_size`.\n\n```\n# This concatenates the sharded checkpoints and makes it easier for us to load.\npython models/tt_transformers/scripts/repack_weights_70b.py <path_to_checkpoint_dir> <repacked_output_dir>\n```\n\nIf providing a different output directory, please copy the `params.json` and the `tokenizer.model` files to the new directory.\n\n**⚠️ Warning**\n>\n> For Llama3 models, weights downloaded from the `huggingface-cli` via\n>```\n>huggingface-cli download meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-70B-Instruct --include \"original/*\" --local-dir Meta-Llama-3-70B-Instruct\n>```\n> will be in the same format as a direct download from Meta (i.e. as `consolidated.xx.pth` files). Hence, you will still need to repack your weights and export `LLAMA_DIR` as before. This is contrary to if you downloaded your weights directly from `huggingface`, as those weights will be downloaded as sharded `.safetensors` files.\n\n#### You are all set!\n\n- Skip to section: [Run the Demo](#run-the-demo)\n\n---\n\n#### Option 2: Download Weights from HuggingFace\n\nNavigate to [HuggingFace](https://huggingface.co) and download the weights of the model you wish to run (check [models chart](#tt-transformers) for compatibility and direct links to HuggingFace models).\n\n- Ensure your model directory has the following structure:\n```\n/path_to/org/model/\n    config.json\n    generation_config.json\n    model-00001-of-00062.safetensors\n    ...\n```\n\n- Set `HF_MODEL` to the directory of the downloaded weights:\n```\nexport HF_MODEL=<path_to_downloaded_directory>\n```\n\n#### You are all set!\n\n- Skip to section: [Run the Demo](#run-the-demo)\n\n---\n\n### Run the Demo\n\n- Make sure either `HF_MODEL` or `LLAMA_DIR` has been set:\n\n`export HF_MODEL=<hf_model_name or hf_downloaded_directory>`\n\n`export LLAMA_DIR=<path_to_meta_downloaded_model_directory>`\n\n- Run the Demo\n\nThese are some example commands on how to run the demo. For more information about the parameters, check [parameters description.](#parameters-description)\n\n```\n# Batch-1\npytest models/tt_transformers/demo/simple_text_demo.py -k \"performance and batch-1\"\n\n# Batch-32\npytest models/tt_transformers/demo/simple_text_demo.py -k \"performance and batch-32\"\n\n# Long context with custom parameters\npytest models/tt_transformers/demo/simple_text_demo.py -k \"long-context\" --max_seq_len=16384\n\n# Long-context\npytest models/tt_transformers/demo/simple_text_demo.py -k \"performance and long\"\n```\n\nThe above examples are run in `ModelOptimizations.performance` mode. You can override this by setting the `optimizations` or the `decoder_config_file` argument in the demo. To use instead the accuracy mode you can call the above tests with `-k \"accuracy and ...\"` instead of performance.\n\n## Details\n\n### Extra compatibility settings for non-Llama models\n\nIf you are bringing up a new model that is similar to these but is not listed above, you may also need to set additional environment variables:\n- `MAX_PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE` - this determines how many thousands of tokens are prefilled in one go. For optimal performance pick 128. Depending on the model dimensions and hardware you're running on, there may not be enough L1 to prefill 128K tokens at once, in which case you can reduce this in powers of 2 down to 4.\n- `PAD_MLP_CORES` - models with a hidden_dim that is not a nice power of 2 may not have a valid layout or may run with lower performance. You can set this to a multiple of 8 between 8 and 64; `16` and `32` commonly work well if this is required.\n\nYou should also watch out for:\n- RoPE encoding style. `llama3`, `yarn` and of course `none` are supported. HuggingFace models encode the complex numbers in RoPE as r1, r2, ..., i1, i2, ... whereas Meta models encode the complex numbers as r1, i1, r2, i2, ... - TTT uses a Meta-style implementation of the RoPE op and when loading a HuggingFace it will reshuffle the weights of the pre-rope attention weights to interleave their outputs in this style (see `reverse_permute` in [load_checkpoints.py](tt/load_checkpoints.py)). When _using_ TTT this happens invisibly and should not affect you, but when bringing up a new model or modifying TTT being aware of this will make some otherwise confusing things clearer.\n- Our [accuracy test](tests/test_accuracy.py) will require you to [generate some reference logits](tests/generate_reference_hf.py) and perhaps update the test to use them.\n- We parallelise attention over the number of heads. If this number is e.g. 14 then you will not be able to run it on more than 2 chips (because 14/2=7, a prime number). We do not support head-padding or similar mitigations at this time but a PR would be cool.\n\nHuggingface models specify their architecture in the `config.json` file. The following architectures are known to work:\n\n- LlamaForCausalLM\n- Qwen2ForCausalLM\n- Qwen3ForCausalLM\n- MistralForCausalLM\n- Phi3ForCausalLM\n\nAt the time of writing this covers the majority of popular HuggingFace text-generation models. If you find another architecture that works or extend TT-Transformers to support one we would love to accept a PR!\n\n---\n\n### Environment Variables Description\n\n- `HF_MODEL` is the HuggingFace org/name of the model you want to run or the path to the downloaded Huggingface weights.\n- `LLAMA_DIR` sets the path for Meta-provided Llama3 model weights if you are not using HuggingFace.\n- `TT_CACHE_PATH` is optional. It sets the path for ttnn's weight cache files. See below for more details.\n- `MESH_DEVICE` is optional. It allows you to use fewer devices than are available. See below for more details.\n\nOn the first execution of each model, TTNN will create weight cache files for that model, to speed up future runs. These cache files only need to be created once for each model and device. These files are stored in one of three places:\n\n1. `TT_CACHE_PATH` if you have set it.\n2. `HF_MODEL/device_name` if a path to downloaded weights was specified using `HF_MODEL`.\n3. `LLAMA_DIR/device_name` if a path to downloaded Meta-provided weights was specified using `LLAMA_DIR`.\n4. `model_cache/HF_MODEL/device_name` if a HuggingFace model name was specified using `HF_MODEL`.\n\nThe device name used is:\n\n- `N150` for N150\n- `N300` for N300\n- `T3K` for LoudBox / QuietBox\n- `TG` for Galaxy\n\nBy default tensor parallelism is used to run the model over all available chips. You can instead run on a smaller mesh either for testing or for performance reasons (for very small models the communication overhead of tensor parallelism may be larger than the performance gained). To use a smaller mesh, set `MESH_DEVICE` to one of the supported devices: `N150`, `N300`, `T3K` or `TG`.\n\nExample: `export MESH_DEVICE=N150`, will enable running one a single chip of a multi-chip system.\n\n---\n\n### Parameters Description\n\nThe `simple_text_demo.py` script includes the following main modes of operation and is parametrized to support other configurations.\n\n- `batch-1`: Runs a small prompt (128 tokens) for a single user\n- `batch-32`: Runs a small prompt (128 tokens) for a a batch of 32 users\n- `long-context`: Runs a large prompt (64k tokens) for a single user\n- `reasoning-1`: Runs a reasoning prompt for a single user (generates up to 15k tokens)\n\nIf you want to provide your own demo configuration, please take a look at the pytest parametrize calls in `models/tt_transformers/demo/simple_text_demo.py`. For convenience we list all the supported params below:\n\n- `input_prompts (string)`: input json file with prompts to process. See `models/tt_transformers/demo/*.json` for a list of input files\n- `instruct (bool)`: Whether to use Llama instruct weights or general weights\n- `repeat_batches (int)`: Number of consecutive batches of users to run (default: 1)\n- `max_seq_len (int)`: Maximum context length supported by the model (refer to the table above)\n- `batch_size (int)`: Number of users in a batch (Supports 1/2/4/8/16/32 batches)\n- `max_generated_tokens (int)`: Maximum number of tokens to generate for each user (Note that the users will stop generation before this limit if they reach a eos token)\n- `paged_attention (bool)`: Whether to use paged attention or default attention (vLLM support (WIP) requires paged attention)\n- `page_params (dict)`: Page parameters for paged attention - [`block_size`, `max_num_blocks`]. For smaller context lengths use `block_size=32` and `max_num_blocks=1024`, for larger context use block_size=64 and max_num_blocks=2048\n- `sampling_params (dict)`: Sampling parameters for decoding -[`temperature`, `top_p`]. If temperature is set to 0, argmax (greedy decode) is used.\n- `stop_at_eos (bool)`: Flag to stop decoding when the model generates an EoS token\n- `optimizations (ModelOptimizations)`: Optimization level to use for the model [`accuracy`, `performance`]. Applied uniformly across all decoders unless an override config exists in `models/tt_transformers/model_params/<model-name>`\n- `decoder_config_file (DecodersPrecision)`: Fine-grained optimization control that allows specifying a configuration file to set different settings for each decoder.\n\nPlease note that using `argmax` with `batch_size > 1` or using `top-p` sampling with any batch size, these ops will be run on host. This is because those ops are not yet fully supported on device. A decrease in performance is expected when these configurations are enabled.\n\n---\n\n### Optimization overrides\nSome models require a unique set of optimizations defined in `models/tt_transformers/model_params/<model-name>`. To override the default optimizations, you can define files named `models/tt_transformers/tt/model_config/PERFORMANCE_DECODER_CONFIG_FILENAME` and `models/tt_transformers/tt/model_config/ACCURACY_DECODER_CONFIG_FILENAME` in the appropriate `models/tt_transformers/model_params/<model-name>` directory to override the `ModelOptimizations.performance` and `ModelOptimizations.accuracy` optimizations respectively. For example, to override the default \"performance\" optimizations for Llama3.1-8B-Instruct, a file named `performance_decoder_config.json` has been created in the `models/tt_transformers/model_params/Llama3.1-8B-Instruct` directory. The content to write in override files is described in [the custom optimizations section](#custom-optimizations). Optimizations are applied with the following prioritization:\n1. from override config (if it exists)\n2. from the `optimizations` argument\n\n---\n\n### Custom input arguments\nTo facilitate testing different configurations, `simple_text_demo.py` supports argument overrides. The full list of overrides is included in `models/tt_transformers/demo/conftest.py`.\n\nAn example usage where the `batch-1` test is modified to run with 16 users and keep generating tokens until 1024 are generated:\n\n```\npytest models/tt_transformers/demo/simple_text_demo.py -k \"performance and batch-1\" --batch_size 16 --max_generated_tokens 1024 --stop_at_eos 0\n```\n\n---\n\n### Custom optimizations\nTo apply the same settings across all decoders, the `optimizations` argument can be used. `optimizations` offers a wide range of configurations for precision and math fidelity. The user can override the configurations of the data types of the weight tensors and activation tensors and the math fidelity of the kernels that works on those tensors, using the `--optimizations` argument on the command line. For example:\n\n```\npytest models/tt_transformers/demo/simple_text_demo.py -k \"accuracy and batch-1\" --optimizations 'precision_cfg = {ff1_3: bfp4, ff2: bfp4, wqkv: bfp8, wo: bfp8, kv_cache: bfp8, activation: mixed}, fidelity_cfg = {li_ff1_3: hifi2, li_ff2: lofi, li_qkv_decode: hifi2, li_o_decode: hifi2, sdpa_decode: hifi2na, li_qkv_prefill: hifi2, li_o_prefill: hifi2fp16, sdpa_prefill: hifi4}'\n```\n\nPlease refer to [model_config.py](models/tt_transformers/tt/model_config.py) for the full list of supported key-value pairs in the `--optimizations` argument. Also, please refer to the [PERF.md](PERF.md) file for performance and accuracy across a select range of configurations for an example Pareto front analysis.\n\nTo apply non-uniform settings across the decoders, the user can provide a JSON file using the `decoder_config_file` argument to specify the configuration for each decoder. For example\n\n```\npytest models/tt_transformers/demo/simple_text_demo.py -k \"performance and batch-1\" --decoder_config_file 'models/tt_transformers/demo/config_16_decoders.json'\n```\n\nWhen a component is not specified (e.g., FF2 is missing for decoder 2 in `models/tt_transformers/demo/config_16_decoders.json`), the baseline configuration is used for that component.\n\nUsing the lt tool (`models/tt_transformers/lt`), the user can also provide multiple JSON configurations in the `models/tt_transformers/tests/configurations` folder and run a Pareto analysis on them using the `pareto_from_json` command.\n\n---\n\n### Expected performance and accuracy\n\nSee [PERF.md](PERF.md) for expected performance and accuracy across different configurations.\nAccuracy of the network architectures is measured by exact token matching using teacher forcing method. During inference the previous token is replaced by the ground truth token while the network generates the next token. This allows to avoid accumulating errors when comparisons on a finer level (tokens) assessed in comparison to other known metrics that compare quality and context of the answer. Token accuracy can be reported by passing the argument shown below:\n\n```\npytest models/tt_transformers/demo/simple_text_demo.py -k \"performance and batch-1\" --token_accuracy True\n```\n\n---\n\n### Implementation notes\n\n**Chunked prefill (text-only)**: All of the compatible model/device combinations support a max prefill context-length of 128k, with the exception of Llama3.1-8B and Llama3.2-11B on N150 which have a max of 64k (due to a lack of memory). To support these large max context-lengths, chunked prefill is performed with different max chunk sizes as shown in the table below.\n\nMax Prefill Chunk Sizes (text-only):\n|              |      N150     |      N300     |      T3K       |      TG     |\n|--------------|---------------|---------------|----------------|-------------|\n| Llama3.2-1B  | 128k tokens   | 128k tokens   | 128k tokens    | 128k tokens |\n| Llama3.2-3B  | 8k tokens     | 128k tokens   | 128k tokens    | 128k tokens |\n| Qwen2.5-7B | 4k tokens | 32k tokens | 128k tokens | 128k tokens |\n| Llama3.1-8B  | 4k tokens     | 64k tokens    | 128k tokens    | 128k tokens |\n| Llama3.2-11B | 4k tokens     | 64k tokens    | 128k tokens    | 128k tokens |\n| Llama3.1-70B | Not supported | Not supported | 32k tokens     | 128k tokens |\n| Llama3.2-90B | Not supported | Not supported | 32k tokens     | Not supported |\n| DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama3.3-70B | Not supported | Not supported | 32k tokens | 128k tokens |\n\n\n- These max chunk sizes are specific to max context length 128k and are configured via `MAX_PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZES_DIV1024` in [model_config.py](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/models/demos/llama3/tt/model_config.py). If the max context length is set to a smaller value using the `max_seq_len` flag (see [Run the demo](#run-the-demo)), these chunk sizes can possibly be increased due to using a smaller KV cache.\n\n**Chunked prefill (Llama3.2-11B multimodal)**: Llama3.2-11B multimodal is currently only supported on N300 and T3000. On N300, a max prefill context length of 8k is supported, while T3000 supports a max context length of 128k.\n\n---\n\n### Memory Optimization\n\n#### HuggingFace Model Caching Control\n\nTo help manage memory usage, you can control whether the HuggingFace model is cached in memory using the `cache_hf` parameter via command line or code:\n\n```python\n# Default: disables caching to conserve memory usage\nmodel_args = ModelArgs(\n    mesh_device,\n    cache_hf=False,  # Default: Reduces memory usage by not keeping HF model in memory\n    max_batch_size=1,\n    max_seq_len=2048\n)\n\n# Optional: enables caching for faster repeated access\nmodel_args = ModelArgs(\n    mesh_device,\n    cache_hf=True,  # Cache HF model for better performance running reference tests\n    max_batch_size=4,\n    max_seq_len=4096\n)\n```\n\n**When to disable caching (`cache_hf=False`):**\n- Running on systems with limited memory (< 256GB)\n- Loading large models (70B+ parameters)\n- Using the model for single inference runs\n- When you don't need reference model comparisons\n\n**When to keep caching enabled (`cache_hf=True`, default):**\n- Sufficient memory available\n- Comparisons with torch model is needed\n- Minimizing test duration is prioritized over memory usage\n- Running reference model tests\n\nThe `cache_hf` parameter affects:\n- `load_state_dict()` method: Controls whether HF model is cached after loading\n- `reference_transformer()` method: Controls whether to reuse cached model or load fresh\n\n**Memory Impact:**\n- Disabling caching saves approximately the full model size in memory\n- For a 70B model, this can save ~140GB+ of memory usage\n- Increased test duration as model needs to be reloaded for reference operations\n","numLines":429,"startLine":1,"totalLines":429}}}

To obtain a huggingface token visit: https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/security-tokens\n    19→\n    20→## How to Run\n    21→\n    22→### Demo\n    23→Run the demo with sample images:\n    24→```bash\n    25→pytest --disable-warnings models.demos.ttnn_resnet.tests/test_demo.py::test_demo_sample\n    26→```\n    27→Where 16 is the batch size per device, and `models/demos/ttnn_resnet/demo/images/` is where the images are located.\n    28→\n    29→Run with ImageNet dataset:\n    30→```bash\n    31→pytest --disable-warnings models.demos.ttnn_resnet.tests/test_demo.py::test_demo_imagenet\n    32→```\n    33→The 16 refers to batch size per device and 100 is the number of iterations (batches).\n    34→- **T3000**: Processes 100 batches of size 128 total (8 devices × 16 per device), total of 12,800 images\n    35→- **TG**: Processes 100 batches of size 512 total (32 devices × 16 per device), total of 51,200 images\n    36→\n    37→## Testing\n    38→\n    39→### End-to-End Performance\n    40→For end-to-end performance testing, run:\n    41→```bash\n    42→pytest models.demos.ttnn_resnet.tests/test_perf_e2e_resnet50.py::test_perf_trace_2cqs\n    43→```\n    44→This will generate a CSV with the timings and throughputs.\n    45→\n    46→**Expected end-to-end performance:**\n    47→- **T3000**: For batch = 16 per device (128 total), approximately **35,800 fps**\n    48→- **TG**: For batch = 16 per device (512 total), approximately **96,800 fps**\n    49→\n    50→Performance may vary machine to machine.\n    51→\n    52→## Details\n    53→\n    54→+ The entry point to the Metal ResNet model is `ResNet` in `ttnn_functional_resnet50.py`.\n    55→+ The model picks up certain configs and weights from TorchVision pretrained model.
